deliverables.text: An original scatter plot of all twenty flux measurements from Appendix A (time step on the horizontal axis, flux in parts per million on the vertical axis), with the four in-transit points visibly marked apart from the sixteen out-of-transit points.

A calculated line of best fit through the sixteen out-of-transit points only, plotted on top of the D1 scatter plot, plus a written judgment of how strong the correlation between time and flux really is and why a single straight line is a poor (non-linear) description of the night's actual drift.

The naive significance ratio: the transit dip's depth (measured against the D2 line, extended into the transit window) divided by the standard deviation of the out-of-transit points' residuals from that line, shown step by step, compared against Appendix B's 3.0 follow-up threshold.

A box-and-whisker plot of the sixteen out-of-transit flux values, with all five summary numbers labeled and the interquartile range shown, plus the distribution-aware significance ratio compared against the same 3.0 threshold, and a note on whether any out-of-transit point qualifies as a statistical outlier by the 1.5×IQR rule.

A one-paragraph written recommendation that states both significance numbers from D3 and D4, explains in plain language why a curved, non-linear drift makes a straight-line read and a distribution-based read disagree, and names which read the student trusts more and why.

appendices.title: The Marginal Candidate's Overnight Light Curve
Two Significance Reads and the Follow-Up Threshold

balance.argument_a: Under Method 1 (the naive line-of-best-fit read), the dip's significance is 230.56 ppm ÷ 76.71 ppm = 3.006σ — just clearing the Sable Peak Survey's 3.0 follow-up threshold (Appendix B, MA2). Option A's case is that the survey's own stated policy is written in terms of exactly this kind of significance ratio, the candidate clears it under the most commonly taught method (fit a trend, measure the residual), and declining a slot on a candidate that meets the stated bar risks quietly raising the bar without ever saying so.
balance.argument_b: Under Method 2 (the distribution-aware box-and-whisker read), the same dip's significance is 213.5 ppm ÷ 84.69 ppm = 2.521σ — below the 3.0 threshold. Option B's case is that Appendix A's baseline is visibly non-linear (a curved, not straight, drift across the night), so a straight-line fit is the wrong tool: it can't tell the difference between 'real leftover noise' and 'shape my straight line failed to capture,' and folds both into one deceptively large or small residual figure. The box-and-whisker read never assumes a shape at all — it just asks how unusual the dip looks against the plain, honest spread of a normal night — and by that more conservative, assumption-light read, this candidate does not clear the bar.
balance.margin_basis: margin = (winner - loser) / loser × 100, the corpus-standard convention tier2_probes.py's probe_sensitivity and sensitivity_model.py both use, applied here to the two computed significance values themselves (sig_naive treated as 'A's reading, sig_robust as 'B's reading, per sensitivity_model.py's evaluate()). sig_naive = 230.56/76.71 = 3.0056. sig_robust = 213.5/84.69 = 2.5210. winner = 3.0056 (higher reading), loser = 2.5210. margin = (3.0056-2.5210)/2.5210 × 100 = 0.4846/2.5210 × 100 = 19.2%. This is within SPEC §2's 20% cap (though close to it, deliberately — see sensitivity_disclosure[]), and it straddles the case's own 3.0 decision threshold: sig_naive clears it, sig_robust does not, which is what makes the dilemma genuinely live rather than a rounding difference. NOTE: MA1 (the light curve's exact 20 values) and MA2 (the 3.0 threshold) are both stated Modeling Assumptions — this margin, and which side of 3.0 each method lands on, is a designed property of those chosen values, not an empirical finding about any real star.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The candidate's full 20-point overnight light curve (Appendix A)
modeling_assumptions.value_used: See Appendix A for all 20 flux values; 4-point transit window at t=8-11 (minutes 120-165)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No survey publishes a specific still-unconfirmed candidate's raw per-point pipeline output. The noise level (point-to-point scatter on the order of 50-130 ppm) is bounded by TESS's own published precision figures for a bright target [S1], and the transit dip depth is set roughly 100x smaller than a real confirmed transit's depth [S5], deliberately, to construct a genuinely marginal case.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: sensitivity_model.py's ±50% flex sweep (mechanical, FLEX[]) found the naive-vs-robust ORDERING never flips (sig_naive reads higher than sig_robust at every flexed value, since the fixed drift/noise shape makes the naive method's residual-SD denominator smaller than the robust method's IQR-based denominator at any dip size) — but a -50% flex DOES breach the SPEC §2 20% margin cap (24.5%, vs. the base case's 19.2%). Separately, and more importantly for the dilemma itself: a qualitative threshold-crossing check (not part of the mechanical FLEX[] win/lose test) shows -50% makes BOTH methods fall below the 3.0 threshold (both agree: abandon) and +50% makes BOTH clear it (both agree: re-observe) — the base case is deliberately tuned to the narrow middle band where the two methods land on opposite sides of the line. See sensitivity_disclosure[].

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Sable Peak Survey's own follow-up significance threshold (Appendix B)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public survey policy document states any specific survey's own internal follow-up bar. Set well below Kepler's real, formal 7.1σ discovery threshold [S2], since a follow-up observation only requests more evidence rather than announcing a discovery.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Held fixed in sensitivity_model.py's FLEX[] — changing the threshold does not change which of the two computed significance readings is numerically larger (the mechanical win/lose test evaluate() runs), the same 'structural, not a dial to flex' situation as cases/the-approval-gate/sensitivity_model.py's own gate thresholds. Its real sensitivity is qualitative and threshold-crossing-based, not order-based: at base dip depth, a threshold anywhere in roughly [2.8, 3.0] keeps the two methods disagreeing (the live tension); at or below roughly 2.5 both methods agree the candidate clears it, and at or above roughly 3.1 both agree it does not. See sensitivity_disclosure[].

derived.notes: Figures computed directly from the Appendix A dataset (see sensitivity_model.py), kept here so FACILITATOR.md's Guide Notes stay checkable against a value of record.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public source publishes this specific still-unconfirmed candidate's real dip depth (MA1) — the true figure would exist in principle once the candidate is confirmed or dropped, but is not knowable in advance. Tier 2 P5 (mechanical, sensitivity_model.py evaluate()) found the naive-vs-robust ORDER is stable under ±50% flex (sig_naive always reads higher than sig_robust for this fixed drift/noise shape, so the win/lose test never flips) — but a -50% flex breaches the SPEC §2 20% margin cap (24.5% vs. the base 19.2%). A SEPARATE qualitative check (not part of the mechanical win/lose test, but directly relevant to the actual dilemma) confirms both methods fall below the 3.0 threshold at -50% depth (both agree: abandon) and both clear it at +50% (both agree: re-observe) — the base case is deliberately tuned to the narrow middle band where the two methods land on opposite sides of the survey's own decision line.

No public survey policy sets this figure (MA2) — it is Sable Peak's own internal, undocumented-in-public bar. NOT swept by sensitivity_model.py's FLEX[] (it cannot change which of the two significance readings is numerically larger, so the mechanical win/lose test is structurally insensitive to it — see modeling_assumptions[MA2].sensitivity). A separate qualitative check, run directly against the base-case readings (sig_naive=3.006, sig_robust=2.521), shows a threshold anywhere in roughly [2.8, 3.0] keeps the two methods disagreeing (the live tension this case is built around); at or below ~2.5 both methods agree the candidate clears it; at or above ~3.1 both agree it does not — only the case's own chosen value of exactly 3.0 sits in the narrow window where the two methods disagree at all.
